Maurice Richard, nicknamed The Rocket, was a Canadian right-winger and icon of the Montreal Canadiens who dominated the NHL from the nineteen forties through the nineteen fifties. The first player to score fifty goals in a season, he became a national hero in Quebec and a pioneer of modern hockey aggression and passion.

He scored five hundred forty-four goals in nine hundred seventy-eight regular-season games, a goal-per-game ratio nearly unmatched in his era, and added eighty-two playoff goals, many in crucial moments. He was the first player to score fifty goals in a single season in nineteen forty-four to forty-five, doing so in just fifty games, a benchmark that defined excellence for generations. Richard won six Stanley Cups with the Montreal Canadiens in nineteen forty-three, nineteen forty-four, nineteen forty-six, nineteen fifty-three, nineteen fifty-six, and nineteen fifty-seven, establishing the franchise's early dominance.

He was known for his fierce competitive fire, intensity, and willingness to fight. His temper and stick-work drew criticism and suspensions. He served as captain of the Canadiens for much of his career, and his retirement at age thirty-four was mourned as an end to an era. Richard wore number nine and became the symbol of French-Canadian pride in professional hockey. The Richard Riot of nineteen fifty-five occurred when his suspension sparked protests in Montreal, highlighting his cultural significance.
